Frugality
frū-găl´ĭ-ty
n. (prudent economy; a good husbandry of what one has been given)
Latin frugalitas, from frux, fruit or produce — a frugal man is a fruitful one, who gets increase out of what he has. The root is agricultural, not miserly.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Frugality is good husbandry. The Lord practises it after feeding five thousand from a boy's lunch: “Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost” (John 6:12) — abundance and thrift in the same miracle. Proverbs contrasts the two habits: “There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up” (Pro 21:20), and describes accumulation by increments: “he that gathereth by labour shall increase” (Pro 13:11). The ant is set as a teacher: she “provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest” (Pro 6:8). And the floor of contentment is set low: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines frugality as prudent economy; good husbandry or housewifery; a sparing use or appropriation of money or commodities; and notes that frugality is not parsimony.

expand to see more

FRUGALITY, n. Prudent economy; good husbandry or housewifery; a sparing use or appropriation of money or commodities; a judicious use of any thing to be expended or employed.

Without frugality none can be rich, and with it few would be poor.

2. A prudent and sparing use or appropriation of any thing; as frugality of praise.

FRUGAL, a. Economical in the use or appropriation of money, goods or provisions of any kind; saving unnecessary expense.

Key Scripture

John 6:12 — "When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost."

Pro 21:20 — "There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up."

Pro 13:11 — "Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase."

Pro 6:8 — "Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest."

1Ti 6:8 — "And having food and raiment let us be therewith content."

Modern Corruption

Frugality hardens into meanness, and the same verse that commends saving commends it as a way to have something to give.

expand to see more

John 6:12 is the passage that keeps this virtue from being a temperament. The One who had just created bread out of nothing, for a crowd of thousands, then tells His disciples to gather up the fragments that nothing be lost — and they filled twelve baskets. Infinite supply and careful economy in the same afternoon, from the same Person. Frugality is therefore not a hedge against scarcity or a symptom of anxiety; it is a right relation to things that have been given, and the giver's generosity does not cancel it.

The corruption is meanness, and Scripture is alert to it. Proverbs elsewhere describes the man who hasteth to be rich and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him, and the one who withholdeth more than is meet and it tendeth to poverty. Ephesians 4:28 gives the purpose that keeps saving honest: let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth. Increase is aimed at generosity. A frugality that terminates on a balance has become the thing it was supposed to serve.

The other corruption is the modern one, and it is not stinginess but drift. Proverbs 13:11 describes wealth gotten by vanity diminishing, and the man who gathers by labour increasing — and the mechanism in both directions is incremental. Nobody decides to have nothing at fifty; small leaks do it, and small deposits reverse it. Webster's line is worth keeping: without frugality none can be rich, and with it few would be poor. It is a proverb about arithmetic, and it is still true.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek klasma (G2801), a fragment; apollumi (G622), to be lost, perish; Hebrew qabats (H6908), to gather; otsar (H214), treasure, store.

expand to see more

Greek klasmata (G2801) — fragments, broken pieces; John 6:12–13, Matthew 14:20, Mark 8:19–20.

Greek hina me ti apoletai (G622) — that nothing be lost; John 6:12.

Hebrew otsar nechmad (H214) — treasure to be desired; Proverbs 21:20, 15:6, 8:21.

Usage

"“Gather up the fragments… that nothing be lost” — after creating bread from nothing."

"“He that gathereth by labour shall increase” — by increments, both ways."

"“That he may have to give to him that needeth” — what the saving is for."
